preamble: Loss of the voiceless uvular stop [q] is attested in Austronesian. Proto-Malayo-Polynesian *q, reconstructed as a uvular stop, was lost without trace in many Western Malayo-Polynesian languages: PMP *qatay 'liver' gives Malagasy aty, Tagalog atáy, Javanese ati and Buginese ate, and PMP *quzan 'rain' gives Malagasy órana and Javanese udan. In Oceanic, Proto-Oceanic *q disappeared in Fijian and many Southeast Solomonic languages (POc *qupi 'yam' > Fijian uvi, Gela uvi). Other daughters stopped at a glottal stop: Cebuano bagʔú 'new' and Palauan ʔad 'liver' keep [ʔ], Malay has h (hati, hujan), and Polynesian *q was [ʔ] before being lost in Samoan. The Arabic qāf > [ʔ] change also ends in a glottal stop. Those outcomes belong under q_to_glottal_stop.

examples.note: Initial *q lost; Malagasy final -y is orthographic [i].
Initial *q lost; Malagasy adds a final -a after a final consonant.
Tagalog vowel-initial words have a predictable [ʔ] onset, so the medial case is clearer.
Medial *q lost with no trace. Compare Cebuano bagʔú, which keeps a glottal stop.
Compare Malay hati, which keeps *q as h.
Old Javanese also udan; compare Malay hujan.
Initial *q lost with no glottal reflex; *p > v.
Also Bughotu and Simbo uvi, Kwaio ufi.
